transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess… I came in because I just don’t see things getting back on track anymore. The studio, my life, all of it. I keep thinking if I work harder or if they set up some payment plan, maybe it’ll fix something, but honestly it feels like none of that matters. Like it’s already too far gone.
Have you been feeling sad or empty most of the time lately?

Yeah… most days, I’d say. I wake up and it’s like this heavy gray thing is already there before I even get my boots on. And then I get to the shop—wood everywhere, tools, stuff I used to actually enjoy being around—and it just feels… flat. Like I’ll catch myself just standing there staring instead of doing anything. I don’t know, it’s hard to explain.
Do you still enjoy activities that you used to find pleasurable?

I mean… I don’t know. Some things, maybe? I used to like getting into a project, shaping a piece just right, but lately I can’t really tell if I’m not enjoying it or if I’m just distracted by everything going wrong. Like, even when I pick up a tool, I start thinking about invoices or this old cabinet job from years ago where the client kept changing the plans, and then I’m off in my head instead of noticing whether I liked doing it. So… I’m not sure how to answer that exactly.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in?

I’m not really sure. I try to think of something and my mind kind of wanders off. Like, I used to sit outside after work sometimes, just watch the neighborhood quiet down, and now I’ll sit there and start noticing the fence needs fixing or remembering some job I didn’t finish the way I wanted. So I don’t know if that counts as pleasure. It’s more like… passing time, I guess.
Have you noticed any changes in your weight recently?

I haven’t really kept track, to be honest. My pants fit about the same, I think… though some days I don’t even notice that kind of thing. I’ll get dressed for work and then start thinking about whether I left a clamp set up wrong or if I need to pick up more screws, and by the time I’m out the door I couldn’t tell you. So… no, I don’t think I’ve noticed anything clear with my weight.
Have you been having trouble sleeping lately?

I don’t know… sleep’s kind of hard to pin down. Some nights I get in bed and then I start thinking about whether I measured something wrong on a job, or I remember I need to sharpen a blade, and then I’m just lying there thinking instead of noticing the time. But I couldn’t tell you if it’s been worse lately exactly. I haven’t really been keeping track.
Have you been feeling unusually tired lately?

Yeah… tired is probably the right word. It’s strange, because I’m not always doing much more than usual, but by midmorning my arms feel like I’ve already been hauling lumber all day. I’ll be measuring something, or trying to make a cut, and I’m just… wiped out.

Even if I’ve been in bed all night, I don’t feel like I’ve got much in the tank. Returning a couple calls feels like more work than it should. Then I start thinking I should organize the back of the truck, and there’s that one box of old hinges I keep meaning to sort, but I just kind of stand there looking at it. So, yeah. Pretty tired.
Have you had any thoughts about not wanting to live or hurting yourself?

I… I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, “not wanting to live” sounds like a big thing when you say it that way, and I don’t know if I’ve really sat there and put it in those words.

Hurting myself… I don’t know. I haven’t really thought it through like that. My mind usually goes off to practical stuff, like what needs fixing or what I forgot to load in the truck, and then I lose the thread. So… I guess I’m not sure what I’d call it.
Have you had any thoughts about hurting yourself?

I don’t… I don’t really know. Hurting myself like on purpose? I guess I haven’t sat down and made some kind of plan or anything.

Sometimes when I’m working I’ll notice a chisel is dull, and then I’m thinking about how I should’ve taken better care of my tools, and then that turns into thinking about how everything I do is half-finished… but that’s not exactly what you’re asking.

So… I’m not sure. I don’t think I have a clear answer.
Have you experienced a loss of interest in most activities for most of the day?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I mean… “most activities” is a lot to sort through. Work is work, you know, some days I’m into it and some days I’m just trying to get the boards cut straight and not mess up the measurements.

Like, I used to spend forever looking at different kinds of wood grain—oak, maple, all that—and now if a customer wants something specific, I just try to match it and move on. But that might just be because I’ve done it for so long. After twenty-some years, not everything feels special.

So… I don’t know. I haven’t really been keeping track of whether I’m interested or not for most of the day. I guess I’d need you to explain what you mean a little more.
How long have you been feeling this way?

I guess… if I’m trying to put a date on it, it started after I took on the mortgage for the studio. That was a little over two years ago now.

It’s funny, I remember signing all that paperwork and thinking more about whether the place had enough outlets for the tools than about the money, and then later it was like… every month there it was. Anyway—yeah, about two years and two months, something like that.
How long have you felt like you've lost interest in the things you used to enjoy?

It’s been… pretty much since I took on the mortgage for the studio. I keep coming back to that, I guess, because that’s when things started feeling different.

That was a little over two years ago now—about two years and two months, maybe. Funny what sticks in your head… I remember worrying about where I’d put the clamps more than the loan itself, and then after that everything I used to enjoy just kind of got harder to care about.
Would you say your feelings of sadness are mild, or are they interfering with your daily life more significantly?

It’s… it’s more than mild, I think. Most days I wake up and it’s like this heavy gray feeling is already there before I even get my boots on.

And I’ll be in the shop, with all the wood around me—stuff I used to really notice, like the grain and the smell when you cut into it—and it just feels flat. Sometimes I catch myself just standing there, staring, and I have to make myself move. So yeah… I’d say it gets in the way.
Would you say these feelings of sadness are affecting your daily life most of the time?

Yeah… most of the time, I’d say. It’s there when I wake up, like this heavy gray thing already sitting on me before the day even starts.

I’ll get into the shop and it’s strange, because the wood used to kind of pull me in—you know, the smell of it, the grain, figuring out a cut. My dad used to say you could tell good walnut by the way it almost looked wet under the light… sorry, that’s not really what you asked. But now I’m standing there around all of it and it just feels flat. Like I have to push myself just to move instead of staring at nothing. So yeah, it affects me most days.
How long have you felt like you've lost interest in the things you used to enjoy, has it been the full two years since taking on the mortgage or has it varied over time?

Yeah… I’d say it’s been pretty steady since then. Since I took on the studio mortgage, a little over two years ago now—about two years and two months.

I mean, there are little moments here and there where I get distracted, like if I’m sharpening a chisel just right or I’m trying to remember where I left a box of old hinges… I’ve got this one drawer that’s just a disaster. But the not-caring part, the loss of interest, that’s been there the whole time, really. Since the mortgage.
Would you describe your current feelings of sadness as moderate or severe?

Severe, I guess… yeah. Most days I wake up and it’s already there, this heavy gray feeling sitting on me before I’ve even done anything.

And in the shop, I mean, that used to be the place I felt most like myself—wood stacked up, the smell of sawdust, all that—but now it just feels flat. I’ll be standing there with boards around me and I have to fight not to just stop and stare. So… yeah, I’d call it severe.
